question: to the Commission Marianne Vind (S&D), Vilija Blinkevičiūtė (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Per Clausen (The Left), Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Idoia Mendia (S&D), Alicia Homs Ginel (S&D), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Maria Grapini (S&D), Kira Marie Peter-Hansen (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Christel Schaldemose (S&D), Niels Fuglsang (S&D), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Johan Danielsson (S&D), Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

A recent documentary by the Danish Broadcasting Corporation reveals that four former young medical student assistants developed cancer after working over a prolonged period with formaldehyde. They were all under the age of 35, and three have since tragically passed away. When four young doctors fall ill after working with a known carcinogen, alarm bells should ring. Their stories raise serious concerns about the protection of workers exposed to formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is widely used across Europe – in textiles, plastics, glued wood and embalming – with many workers exposed to it daily. The documentary also exposes a concerning correlation between industry funding and research outcomes, as chemical companies and their lobby organisations have actively sought to shape the scientific basis for the EU’s occupational exposure limit. A former member of the EU scientific committee has stated that the committee’s original recommendation of an exposure limit of 0.2 ppm was likely increased to 0.3 ppm following persistent lobbying pressure. In this context: 1.
Will the Commission launch a new assessment of formaldehyde considering these revelations?
Will it ensure that any reassessment is expedited, and the limit is lowered if new evidence shows higher risks?
How does the Commission take into account industry funding and lobbying when evaluating the scientific evidence underpinning EU exposure limits?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) The process of setting occupational exposure limits (OEL) is set out in Directive 2004/37/EC1. Directive 2019/9832 sets an occupational exposure limit for formaldehyde of 0.3 ppm (parts per million). This was based on a comprehensive evidence-based process which also took into account the views of national authorities and representatives of the employers and workers. The selection of the substances for which to possibly set new or review existing OELs includes a broad consultative approach within the tripartite Advisory Committee on Safety and Health at Work (ACSH), which includes national authorities and social partners. The ACSH regularly provides the Commission with advice for the priority chemicals for which they recommend an OEL, informing the policy-making process. This advice is provided based on the availability of new science and data as brought to the attention of the ACSH working party on ‘Chemicals at the Workplace’ (WPC). The WPC is discussing a possible updated list of chemicals for which they would advise the Commission on setting new or revising existing OEL values. Such an update is expected by mid-2026. The process of setting OELs is evidence-based. It relies on a broad consultation of stakeholders and on the scientific assessment of evidence by independent experts in the risk assessment committee of the European Chemicals Agency. Moreover, the Regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)3 restricts formaldehyde emissions into indoor air to protect consumers4.
